name: Great Lakes Bantu
region: Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, northwestern Tanzania and the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
defining_innovation: The Bantu of the interlacustrine kingdoms (Buganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Nkore), a close group whose largest members, Kinyarwanda and Kirundi, are spoken by almost everyone in their countries.

chapters.title: Kingdoms of the Lakes
chapters.body: Around the great lakes of East Africa, Bantu-speaking farmers built some of the region's most centralised kingdoms: Buganda on the shores of Lake Victoria, and Rwanda and Burundi in the highlands. Their languages, Luganda, Kinyarwanda and Kirundi, belong to a close group together with Haya, Runyankore and others. Nilotic-speaking pastoralists moved into the region over the last thousand years and influenced its societies and some of its languages.

chapters.title: Writing and National Languages
chapters.body: Protestant and Catholic missionaries reached Buganda in 1877–79 and wrote Luganda in the Latin alphabet. A Luganda Bible followed in 1896, and Luganda became the language of the colonial administration in much of Uganda. In Rwanda and Burundi, unusually for African states, a single Bantu language is spoken by nearly the whole population, and Kinyarwanda and Kirundi became national and official languages at independence in 1962.

turning_points.title: The lakes group forms
turning_points.description: Farming communities around the lakes develop into the Great Lakes Bantu group. Later, from the mid-2nd millennium, the Buganda, Rwanda and Burundi kingdoms grow up in the region.

sources.citation: Van de Velde, Mark, Koen Bostoen, Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson, eds. 2019. The Bantu Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Nilotic neighbours
turning_points.description: Nilotic-speaking pastoralists, among them Luo groups, move into the region. Some assimilate to Bantu languages and others stay distinct, and Nilotic vocabulary, especially for cattle, enters the Bantu languages.

sources.citation: Ehret, Christopher. 1998. An African Classical Age: Eastern and Southern Africa in World History, 1000 B.C. to A.D. 400. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia.

turning_points.title: Luganda in writing
turning_points.description: Missionaries in Buganda write Luganda in Latin letters, and the complete Luganda Bible is published in 1896. Luganda becomes a written language of administration and education.

sources.citation: Van de Velde, Mark, Koen Bostoen, Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson, eds. 2019. The Bantu Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: National languages of Rwanda and Burundi
turning_points.description: At independence, Kinyarwanda and Kirundi become national and official languages, spoken by nearly the whole population of each country. That is rare in Africa, where most states have many languages.

sources.citation: Van de Velde, Mark, Koen Bostoen, Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson, eds. 2019. The Bantu Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.
